speechtext: The House resumed from Friday, March 8, consideration of the motion of Mr. Fraser that Bill C-32, an Act to amend the Fisheries Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian Tobin (Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise in my place today to speak on Bill C-32. I am pleased for a number of reasons. This Bill gives us an opportunity to address some outstanding issues in the fishing community, both on the east coast of Canada and, in particular, on the west coast of Canada.

May I interrupt the Hon. Member for just one second. 1 would like to ask a simple question. I understood when we interrupted this debate on Friday that the Hon. Member wanted to rise and ask questions at that point. Is the Hon. Member now asking questions or is he resuming debate?
Just for the formality, may I see if there are any Members who wish to ask questions in the question time remaining. There being no such questions, we will resume debate with the Hon. Member for Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe.
Mr. Speaker, I would have been delighted to ask questions today but the Hon. Member who spoke last is not in the House.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Minister of State (Government House Leader); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: The Hon. Member is not supposed to refer to that fact.

1 do not think it would be proper, given such an excellent first effort by this Member, who is sincere in his concern about the fishery, to question him seeing that he is not here. I am sure the Hon. Government House Leader would agree that is a very proper attitude for a Member from Newfoundland to take.
As I said, 1 am pleased to have an opportunity to address this Bill. I do not think there is anyone in this House of Commons who does not support a request by the Minister to clarify his powers with respect to his ability to allocate fish, be
it on the west coast or on the east coast of Canada. I think all of us recognize that, given the court cases that have occurred and the fact that the Minister's powers are very fuzzy at this time, there is a need for him to be certain what his powers are with respect to the allocation of fish.
That is not the problem, Mr. Speaker. We support the thrust of the Bill. What Members do not support is the notion that the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Fraser) should have the right to allocate fish unimpeded by any body, by any court, by any user group, without first telling Members of this House and, more important, telling the user groups on the west coast and on the east coast what the guidelines and parameters should be respecting the allocation of fish.
On the west coast of Canada, Mr. Speaker, you would appreciate the tremendous value of the salmon fishery worth many hundreds of millions of dollars, some estimate as much as a billion dollars, and you would know there are conflicts between various user groups, between native and non-native fishermen, between commercial and sports fishermen-
Fish people.
The Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell) reminds me I should say fish people-and between fish people of whatever sex.
Oh, oh!

These conflicts are real and the bottom line is that they affect people's ability to make a living. They affect their livelihood, their ability to put bread and butter on the table and their ability to protect, in many cases sometimes, decades of investment by way of gear and vessels and the most modern technology the industry can offer at this time. We have a Minister asking us for approval to clarify his role and his powers to allocate fish without first telling us what the parameters and the guidelines should be with respect to the conflicts between the various user groups. That simply is not acceptable, Sir. We must have a clear statement from the Minister before this House can give approval to a Bill knowing what the consequences of giving the Minister that authority will be.
In my own Province of Newfoundland, there are a number of outstanding issues. I represent a riding, if Members of the New Democratic Party are interested-
Oh, oh!

-on the great northern peninsula of Newfoundland. It is a riding with 500 miles of coastline consisting of
90,000	souls and several hundred communities. In over 50 per

March 11, 1985
Fisheries Act
cent of those communities people live in small villages or towns with populations of under 1,000. 1 know Members will appreciate that in that kind of environment, the fishery, the health of the fishery, the sensitivity of the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, his knowledge and his commitment to the fishery, is critical. It is the difference between having a life of dignity, a life which, if not prosperous, is at least decent, and having no life at all.
The people along that 500 miles of coastline have been trying to organize a meeting with the Minister of Fisheries and his officials in a community called St. Anthony which is located on the tip of the great northern peninsula right on the edge of the Cabot Strait. They pulled together every development association, every fisheries committee and every economic development group along that coastline to have a meeting with the Minister to discuss the establishment of a northern fisheries development corporation. The meeting was scheduled for the end of last month but the Minister, being a busy man and despite the many weeks of preparation, could not attend. Thus the problems and aspirations of the people living on that rocky coastline of the great northern peninsula were put on the shelf. Being the decent people that they are, they did not complain; they simply came back and asked the Minister whether they could schedule another date.
The Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, I am sad to say, as busy as he is, responded last week in the House of Commons by indicating that he could not commit himself to any such meeting or to being in St. Anthony-the outer perimeter of the world, it sounded like to me-but that he would be glad to send some officials. When 30,000 souls along 200 miles of coastline take the trouble for weeks to organize a meeting about the very lifeblood which puts bread and butter on their table, they do not want to meet some official. They know the buck stops with the Minister of Fisheries. They know, because I have told them even though I sit on this side of the House, that the Minister of Fisheries is a good and decent man, if one can simply get his ear. He wants to be an effective Minister of Fisheries. However, they do not know that the Minister has his hands tied by a Minister of Finance who has already slashed in November $31 million from the fisheries budget, by a Minister of Finance who cancelled the $15 million which had been allocated to negotiations between the Province of Newfoundland and the Government of Canada for the establishment of a northern fisheries development corporation on the great northern peninsula.
Hon. Members are probably wondering why we need this northern fisheries development corporation. It is because on the northern peninsula, north of the fiftieth parallel, from the community of Port au Choix all along the peninsula to the Labrador coast and on to the Quebec north shore, historically fishermen and fish plants, as humble as they are, have been nothing but a feeder plant, exporters of raw material. Fishermen bring in some of the best product in the world from some of the richest fishing grounds in the world to a small fish plant. The fish is simply cut, put on ice, loaded on a truck and
exported to Boston. There the product is finished, filleted, packaged and frozen, and it comes back not only to Ottawa, Toronto, Montreal and Vancouver, but to the great northern peninsula as a finished product.
The people on that coast realize that there is something wrong. When they export raw fish, they are not only exporting that product but they are exporting jobs which could and should exist on the great northern peninsula. Each small feeder plant is part of the chain of either a national or international fishing conglomerate. Even though the majority of fish is landed on that coastline in the north, it suits the objectives of multinationals to ship it raw off the northern peninsula and south of the border for packaging.
Fishermen have the raw product and the determination. Given the assistance, the time and the attention of the Minister and of both Governments, they would have the ability within their grasp to take hold of their destiny, to fasten their own sail, to be masters in their own house and to be captain of their own ship. Jobs could be created where they should be, on the great northern peninsula, but that will take our help. If we are going to help, we have to listen. They cannot come to Ottawa. The Minister has to take the time; he has to see it as a high enough priority to go to the great northern peninsula and give these people the fair hearing that they deserve.
There is another matter that upsets me greatly. In the November 8 financial statement by the Minister of Finance the Minister announced that in future berthage fees will be charged to fishermen right across this country. A fisherman who ties up to a public wharf will have to pay a parking fee.
We have the spectacle of this Government having practically put a freeze on small craft harbours funding right across this country, an end to upgrading, maintaining and building new facilities for fishermen on the one hand. On the other hand we have the announcement that fishermen will have to pay to tie up to a wharf. There is a disparity in facilities not only across the regions of this country-some regions have fairly good facilities, some have hardly any-but the disparity within the regions is such that no fair and just berthage fee can be charged to fishermen.
When I was Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance, I had the pleasure of travelling to the great west coast of Canada. At a public wharf, I saw boats lined up 10, 12 and 15 deep. Who will pay the berthage fee? Will it be the fisherman who actually gets to tie up to the wharf who will pay the fee? Will the fellow 15 boats out have to pay when he is not sheltered and protected? According to this regulation, they will all pay.
On the northern peninsula of Newfoundland there is a wharf in the community of Anchor Point where $25 million in fish is landed and taxes are paid. The wharf is falling into the water. Will those fishermen have to pay a berthage fee to tie up to that dilapidated structure? I do not think so. This Government should first establish a basic level of service, a basic quality or standard of harbour facility before deciding to
March 11, 1985

charge fishermen to tie up to facilities which in many cases, if they exist at all, are poor.
Members who were here during the last Parliament will recall the many hours of debate on the bail-out of Fisheries Products International in the Province of Nova Scotia and in the Province of Newfoundland. Some $200 million of government funds was injected to save Nickerson's, National Seed, The Lake Group and Fisheries Products. A new company was formed, Fisheries Products International.
During the time of that debate, the position taken by the Party opposite and by the like-minded Premier of Newfoundland, the Hon. Brian Peckford, who Members opposite will say is a good Conservative, was that no fish plant that was owned by the new conglomerate, Fisheries Products International, could close. Every job had to be saved in every single community. At the time I thought that was a bit ambitious. In fact, I knew it was.
I am bothered now by statements of the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) that Fisheries Products International is for sale. Having injected $200 million of taxpayers' money into that company, having revived the company, having put the company back in operation and beginning the process of making it productive, it will be passed over for a song to private enterprise. They are going to take it back as well as the taxpayers' $200 million. More than that, we are now being told by the federal Government and the Government of Newfoundland that the non-productive plants of Fisheries Products International, and there are several dozen, can be closed. Those communities can be consigned to the dustbin of history. The productive plants, those that are showing a profit when it is sold, will be kept open. I would use an unparliamentary word, Mr. Speaker, but you would simply interrupt my line of thought. Exhibiting concern before September 4 and being brutal immediately afterward is not worthy of the members of the Government.
There are communities both in Nova Scotia and Newfoundland that have been fishing communities for 500 years. There are isolated communities and small towns that have only become accessible by road in the last 15 years though it still takes a drive of a day or two to get to them. There are small towns in which the culture and the way of life have revolved around the fishery. These communities are now being told by the Government, without its offering any alternative suggestion as to how they may provide for themselves otherwise, that their history has been long and colourful but they are about to be consigned to the next chapter of the book on ghost towns in Newfoundland and Nova Scotia. The Minister of Fisheries and Oceans will have to address all of these questions before he finds that members of my Party are prepared to give him the ultimate power to assign quotas for the fish that is available to fishermen and fishing companies.
Let me say in closing that I know the Minister of Fisheries. I have had the pleasure of working with him for the last five years. I know him to be a decent man, a caring man and a
Fisheries Act
sensitive man. However, I know as well that he is a member of a Cabinet that will slash the fishery with no forethought of the consequences in human terms and in terms of isolated communities which have no other options.
On behalf of the Minister and the people I represent, I beg the Minister's Cabinet colleagues to listen to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans because he understands. Because I know the Minister understands and cares, I say to him that if his colleagues will not listen and if the kind of brutal "bull-in-a-china-shop" approach that has been taken so far continues, I would ask the Minister to find the courage and integrity required to do the right thing. He knows that that right thing is to stand up on behalf of his first constituency as Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and to expose the brutal approach to fishermen, their families and their communities that has been taken so far in the brief six months in which this Government has been in power.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Questions or comments?

Mr. Speaker, I must congratulate the Hon. Member on his speech. I would like to ask him a question. The Minister of Fisheries for the Province of Newfoundland has stated publicly that the Government of Newfoundland has made representations to the federal Government about the province's concerns over the federal Government's announcement that it will be terminating the federal fishing vessel insurance program. The union in Newfoundland is also objecting to the termination of this insurance scheme. As of yesterday, the Government of Newfoundland has publicly opposed the cancellation of this scheme.
The provincial Minister of Fisheries has given a public indication that the federal Government is now rethinking this cancellation. He also claims that the federal Government will support the seal hunters and that the federal Government will do this, that and the other thing. I am wondering whether or not the Hon. Member could comment on those items.

It is wonderful what the eminent call of a provincial election will do to wake up the provincial fisheries Minister to the problems which fishermen face in the Province of Newfoundland and Labrador. My fellow colleague, the Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Baker), may or may not know this, but the Premier of Newfoundland has reserved prime time on television and radio tonight. He is going to call an election. Lo and behold, his Ministers in each portfolio, and in particular the Minister of Fisheries, have discovered their clientele, and that all is not rosy and well with Ottawa.
I would say to the Hon. Member opposite that we have not heard a sound from the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans about the $36 million in cut-backs which were announced on November 8 by the Minister of Finance. We have not heard about the introduction of berthage fees, or the cancellation of the vessel subsidy program. Nor have we heard a sound from the Province of Newfoundland about its long-standing state-

March 11, 1985
Fisheries Act
ment that northern cod should only be used for the benefit of Newfoundland and no one else. As a Canadian and a Newfoundlander, that is a position with which I disagree. It has gone by the wayside.
If the politicking between federal and provincial Government was not so obvious, it would be hilarious. Unfortunately, the consequences of that kind of cynical view with respect to fisheries development and management is brutal, not for the politicians who sit in the House, but for the fishermen who live in small communities on the great northern peninsula such as Bear Cove, Anchor Point, Flower's Cove or Cooks Harbour. It is brutal to those fishermen and their families. It is not a laughing matter, it is rather sad.

Mr. Speaker, one of the interesting things which I did not hear the previous speaker elaborate on was how the Liberal Party destroyed the fisheries in Canada. For years and years tremendous opportunities on the west coast laid fallow. I know that the Hon. Member touched on the incompetence of this Government. I wonder if he would care to speak to many of the former Liberal Ministers of Fisheries who did nothing constructive with respect to the West Coast fishery?

Mr. Speaker, it is always interesting that fellows who go to hockey games, sit up in the stands and who have never had a hockey stick in their hands claim to be the biggest experts. We all know the NDP has never formed a government, and will never form a government, so its members are armchair experts in every field of endeavour.
Let me speak about the province which I know best. The reality is, in those districts where the fishing constituency is predominant, Newfoundlanders returned to the House of Commons the Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Baker), the Hon. Member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Rompkey), and myself, the Hon. Member for Humb-er-Port au Port-St. Barbe, despite the best predictions of the pundits. Let me say, in all humility, that I have great respect for the opinions and the decisions of the fishermen of Newfoundland. They decided to send three of us back to the House of Commons in the last election. When the NDP next has the opportunity to hold the hockey stick, its members may then make comments. He who has clean hands has no hands, and I guess the hands of the NDP will stay clean for a long time.

Mr. Speaker, I have a very short comment. I feel certain New Democratic Members will agree that never before in the history of the Government of Canada have we seen so many cuts in such a short period of time as we have recently seen in the Department of Fisheries and Oceans. Never before in the history of the Government of Canada have we seen as many cuts in every federal Department as we have seen in the last few months. There is no comparison-and one could go back to Sir John A. Macdonald-between any former Government and this present Government. It is unfortunate that the New Democratic Party at times is so preoccupied with trying to criticize former Governments that it sometimes loses sight of what is happening today in Canada, and that is what we are dealing with. I would hope that that Party would take
aim at the real issues which face this nation and which have been created by this present Government.

Mr. Speaker, I would just like to follow up on what my hon. colleague has just stated. We have all seen the recent love affair carried on out west with the First Ministers' conference. My hon. friend from Newfoundland has really laid it on the line about the qualities of the federal Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Fraser). I would ask the Hon. Member for Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe (Mr. Tobin) who spoke on this issue if he and the people of Newfoundland do not agree that although the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans might have all of those qualities which were mentioned, he has very little clout in Cabinet and has no influence against this "cut, cut, cut" committee which has been working within the Tory Cabinet? Would the Hon. Member not agree that because the Newfoundland Government has gone along with the love affair we have seen in western Canada, it is in no position now to go back to its own people and say that it fought for the people of Newfoundland? Indeed, it is my two colleagues from Newfoundland who are the ones standing up in this House and defending the rights, privileges and livelihoods of the fishermen in Newfoundland.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member very much for his question. I have one brief comment to make to my colleagues from the New Democratic Party who now profess a sudden interest in the fishery. I noticed with great interest the fact that during the entire summer election campaign, neither the Leader of the New Democratic Party nor any other Hon. Member of that Party visited the Province of Newfoundland even once. Obviously they did not deem it important enough. They did not know enough about the province and they thought it was so insignificant and irrelevant that they didn't even bother to come and visit the province.
Our Leader got elected on the west coast. That Party's Leader did not even take the time to visit the Province of Newfoundland even once during an entire summer election campaign. There can be no more of a stinging indictment than that the New Democratic Party is more interested in holding up the proverbial carrot, promising everything to everybody, rather than taking a serious, mature and realistic approach to problems besetting individuals across this country today.
With respect to his question, I would like to tell my hon. colleague that I believe, as I said earlier, that this Minister of Fisheries and Oceans is a well-intentioned fellow. He is basically a good man. But I feel he is surrounded by Ministers such as the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) who have no knowledge of and, indeed, no sensitivity to the importance of the fishery to both the east coast and the west coast and are prepared to act with a hatchet in dealing with the fishermen on both those coasts. I hope that this Minister of Fisheries and Oceans will emerge as a strong Minister who has clout. I know he has more brains than all of the rest of the Cabinet put together.
March 11, 1985

What I do not know is whether the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has the common sense to recognize that fact. So far he has not. So far the Government has scuttled that Minister and held him up to derision in front of the fishermen of Canada. This Minister is taking flak he does not deserve. He is being blamed for program cuts which he did not initiate. We on this side of the House are trying to help this Minister do his job and be a good Minister, and if Hon. Members opposite cared and would listen, they would get behind this Minister and give him a hand because, basically, he is a good man. But that Minister is in with a crowd of people who belong on the saddle of a robber's horse.

Mr. Speaker, after the Hon. Member's last statement I feel a little winded, to say the least. There is a lot of hot air flowing around this Chamber.
In speaking to Bill C-32, an Act to amend the Fisheries Act,
I want to express the concern which I believe other Hon. Members have expressed that it really is unfortunate that the Minister in this case has made a decision to again centralize the power of the fisheries in his office and in the bureaucracy which in the past have not had a great deal of credibility with the people who are doing the fishing and with the industry as a whole. He has taken it upon himself, without consultation with the people who are directly concerned, to allocate the fish supply.
The intent of the Bill, as I understand it, is to expand the authority of the Minister and the Department of Fisheries and Oceans and in particular to expand the proper management, allocation and control of the sea coast fisheries of Canada. In our view, the Bill gives far too much power to the Minister to allocate the fishery resource. It would seem that this will be controlled largely by the Minister and his staff and undoubtedly would lead to an increase in the bureaucracy which has been far too insensitive, at least at the central level, to the needs of the west coast fisheries in particular. This Bill expands the role of the Department of Fisheries and Oceans personnel and gives them greater authority.
Something I noticed in the Bill which I expect we will agree with is the intent to redefine the term "fish" to include plants. I would hope here that the intent is to expand into various types of fish farming and the farming of sea plants which we know have considerable nutritional value and perhaps export value as well.
The previous speaker remarked on the terminology of the Bill. In preparing for my remarks this morning I found myself once again struggling with the terminology of "fishermen" in view of our charter and wondering what would be a better term. Perhaps we should have a redefinition of that term in this Bill. I considered "fish people", which sounds a little silly, and "fish folk", which sounds a little folksy, but concluded that perhaps we should be using the word "fishers" as a generic term for workers in this industry.
West coast fishers on the whole are a very large community. In the past it has been a very large industry. I would like to
Fisheries Act
give you, Mr. Speaker, a few statistics. The average wholesale value of the Pacific and Yukon fishery management resource between 1979 and 1983 was $45 million. There are some
17,000	commercial fishers and 350,000 to 400,000 recreational fishers. In addition to that, of course, there are many native communities whose main means of survival and potential for economic development is fishing. There are five species of salmon which constitutes the most valuable catch on the west coast. This makes up about 64 per cent of the value of the industry.
The herring and herring roe fishery is a particularly large industry in British Columbia. We are the prime suppliers to the Japanese market and, of course, we have concern about what is happening to our herring fisheries as well as a concern for the salmon fishery. There are many people who work in related industries as well. In my riding of Vancouver East there are many immigrant and native women who get up very early in the morning, while it is still dark, in order to get down to the port to work in the fish canneries and fish freezing industries. Those industries are big job suppliers in my riding and in many others. Potentially, therefore, we have a very strong fishing industry in the Province of British Columbia and potentially it is a self-sufficient industry. It is very important as a renewable resource, but we must take the steps which are needed and which have been so long delayed to have an adequate renewal program.
We know that in recent years there has been a very worrisome shortage of fish on the west coast. This indicates the very urgent need for a proper salmon enhancement program, adequate planning, and the development of new and related industries. I recently saw a very impressive program on TV showing the experiments going on in oyster farming off the northern coast. As the fisher people will tell us, there is a lot that can be done in catching, processing and exporting fish that Canadians do not eat but which other countries, particularly Asian countries, would be very pleased to get in greater numbers, dogfish and hake being two of them. Seaweed and other forms of sea plants are other areas that can and should be developed for a variety of purposes.
There has been an increasing rivalry, given a limited supply of fish on the west coast, between the various user groups seeking the resource. The reduction in available fish has been complicated and perhaps even affected by poor management in the Department of Fisheries and Oceans. I think most people on the west coast who are close to this industry would agree that the lack of adequate planning and consultation with the various groups involved has been a major problem.
My colleague challenged the Liberal Member to look back at the record of the Liberal Government. There is no question at all that the various experts the Liberals used came in with plans and the bureaucracy and the Minister himself just seemed to take their word without consultation with the user groups, and that added greatly to our problems. We had hoped this Minister would be different. As was pointed out, he is

March 11, 1985
Fisheries Act
from the west coast, he is sensitive and I think tries very hard for a just approach in most matters. In view of that, we are very disappointed in this Bill.
I would like to point out that any planning for the fisheries industry must consider human resources as well as the fish resources. The native communities up and down our coast have survived for hundreds or even thousands of years on fish supply. It is the main source of jobs for commercial fishermen and they are very worried. Many of them invested a great deal of money in very expensive vessels and it is critical that they obtain a certain amount of take each year. It is not just the individual fisher people who are affected, it is also their communities. We predict that if these kinds of cut-backs continue along the west coast, many coastal villages will almost disappear. Of course, this affects mothers and children, indeed all the people living in those communities.
We have found that the Liberals were inclined to be very biased toward the sports fishermen. Indeed, this is a big industry. I would not put it at the top of the list myself, but I do know that there is considerable room for expansion if we have more fish so that it is not taking jobs away from commercial fishers and food out of the mouths of native communities.
What is the present Government doing? This Bill was laid on us just as the salmon treaty with the United States was agreed on. There was no consultation with the people who are going to be directly affected and this is very difficult to understand. This Government has talked over and over again about consultation. The Minister himself should certainly be sensitive to this need. The Conservatives promised fair representation and co-operative management in consultation, but where is the consultation? Has there been fair representation in the process involved in presenting this Bill? Once again the Minister did not consult before presenting his plan. He has not gone to the groups most affected despite having promised a more open department. I think there is a considerable concern that again the bureaucrats will be in charge. While we know there are many fine workers in the Public Service, the central bureaucrats have tended to lay some pretty heavy trips on some west coast people and have not been sensitive to their views and needs. So we must ask the Minister to reconsider this and go back to a process which will involve people.
I am not an expert in this field, Mr. Speaker, but the creation of some form of independent board removed from the political sphere seems to make a great deal of sense to me. This was proposed by a lot of people concerned; indeed it was part of the Conservatives' election campaign promises. The board would be outside of political influence entirely and independent of the Department of Fisheries and Oceans. Such a board should consist of members of user groups such as the United Fishermen and Allied Workers' Union in British Columbia. It should include native representatives such as the Native Brotherhood, sports fishers and all those who have a particular interest in this industry, including management. The board should examine the Atlantic and Pacific fisheries stock and determine the size and quality. It should establish a
recommended level of expected return and escapement and the catch levels. It should set quotas and make recommendations on allocations to the Minister. This would take the responsibility away from the Minister and his Department and place it in the hands of the industry.
About a week ago we had a job task force meeting in Vancouver and representatives of the United Fishermen and Allied Workers' Union made a presentation: They said:
The fishing industry in British Columbia is not now nor has it ever been a welfare state for the people who produce its wealth. With our rich salmon resources, the industry has been able to stand on its own two feet although it has experienced its booms and busts. The potential for the industry is being smothered by the bureaucracy and government indifference. Incredible as it may seem, the Department of Fisheries & Oceans is staffed by some 6,000 people nation-wide, when our fishing industries from coast to coast, produce a landed value comparable to a country like Norway (pop. 4.14 million).
Administration of the Pacific fisheries must be de-politicized. The Pacific Fisheries Development Board needs to be created, properly and adequately funded, to develop our fisheries to their fullest potential. The Board's authority would be:
1.	) Arrange loans at reasonable rates of interest to fishermen to finance vessels and gear.
2.	) Selectively reduce the fishing fleets that have an over-capacity for fishing and/or are over-capitalized. Fleet reductions must be voluntary and accomplished by attrition.
3.	) A comprehensive and scientific salmonid enhancement program to concentrate on the enhancement of wild stocks.
4. ) Conduct research with particular reference to coastal and high seas interceptions of salmon. Canada must lay claim to salmon spawned in its streams and rivers and assert ownership over our valuable and fragile salmon resources.
5.	) Develop fisheries and markets for under-utilized or non-utilized species like dogfish and hake.
6.	) Protection of fisheries habitat particularly that for salmon.
These are some of the measures that would be taken to ensure that the fishing industry remains a vibrant and viable part of British Columbia's economy and to ensure that sound management and development policies are being practised for the benefit of the owners of our Pacific fisheries resources- the Canadian people as a whole. I do not understand why there is nothing in the Bill that recommends the establishment of such an interdisciplinary board which would be independent from the Department of Fisheries and Oceans.
There are certain very important principles to the fishing industry that are being threatened by the amendments in this Bill. First, we believe that all users of the resource, including native, commercial and sports fishers, have the right to share in the resource and therefore be involved in the planning and decision-making relating to this resource.
Second, commercial fishers have a right to a fair and decent income for their labour. It is particularly important that they have enough catch and income each year to help pay off their considerable debts for the very expensive vessels that are required in today's fishing industry.
Third, natives have special traditional rights to the resource and to its use in furthering the economic development of their communities. This resource is not only important as a source of food for native people; it is important to their potential
March 11, 1985

development of economic resources in which they may do their own processing as well.
Fourth, while there is potential to develop the sports fishing industry, we hope that it is secondary to the priority of the other two fishing bodies.
Fifth, the protection and enhancement of the resource is paramount and must take priority in all deliberations.
We realize that there are many studies and proposals that have been made which indicate the need for action in this area. Most important is the question of consultation and the reestablishment of some kind of credibility between the Government of Canada and the people on the west coast who both manage and work in this industry.
The allocation of the resource between the various sectors of the industry must be negotiated and developed with the full co-operation and involvement of the industry. Allocation and who controls it is the key to an acceptable plan for fleet rationalization, income stability and resource conservation. Before allocation to the commercial fleet can be even considered, it is necessary to make a commitment to the continued existence of the fleet.
That fleet is very much threatened under the present circumstance. There are fishers who have spent much of last year collecting unemployment insurance. They do not want to be continually dependent on that for their existence. The present circumstances have left many commercial fishers unsure of either their personal future or the future of the fleet as a whole. There is a fear, particularly among smaller independents, that they will be pushed out of the industry. Many of them have already been pushed out of the industry.
There should be a guarantee that fishers, regardless of the type of gear, will have equitable access to the resource in order to maintain a decent income. Emphasis should be placed on the need for consultation and representation on any decisions affecting the industry. The expansion of the powers of the Department of Fisheries and Oceans without sufficient guidelines or curbs, as is being proposed in this Bill, is a common fear among the user groups. I hope that the Minister will meet with the people affected by this legislation and reconsider this Bill, which we and the people affected by it do not like.

Mr. Speaker, there are many concerns about the fishery because the previous Government left it in great difficulty. It did very little for that industry over many years. Furthermore, the bureaucracy under the previous Government was insensitive and unwilling to address the problems facing that industry. The Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell) said that this board might be a better solution to the problem. She outlined some of the duties of that board, but would she expand further to indicate what powers that board should have in order to increase control over the industry?

Mr. Speaker, my colleague knows that I am not an expert in this field. However, I am very concerned about the situation because of its effect on people in my riding,
Fisheries Act
in communities not only in British Columbia but on the east coast, and on those involved in the inland fisheries as well.
I understand that the function of the board would be somewhat different from that of a marketing board. My colleague and I attended a job task force hearing in Saskatoon. It was asked why there could not be a marketing board for the fisheries. It is my understanding that a marketing board would not be necessary because there is no problem with marketing the fish, particularly in our area. The problem is that there is not enough of the resource; it is dwindling and the management of the resource is ineffective.
The most important function of the board would be planning and renewal. Of course, that involves some allocation of the resource but, as I understand it, the problem has been that governments have concentrated too much on limiting the resource without trying to increase it. This is the complaint that I have heard very often. For example, commercial fishermen are not opposed to limiting their catch to a reasonable and fair amount but only want to do so in the knowledge that the resource is being improved and expanded. That would be one of the very important functions of this body. I suggest that the board would be interested in what is taking place in research while keeping close ties with the Department of Fisheries and Oceans in that regard.
I understand that one of the most important aspects of this board would be to bring together all the groups in order to achieve a compromise as a result of conflicting and competing interests due to the shortage of the resource. For example, seiners and gillnetters who have different methods of fishing and are sometimes in competition would have to sit down at the table to negotiate, as would commercial fishers and sports fishers. They would also have to recognize that native people have traditional rights which must be maintained. There would have to be compromise in determining the management and planning of this resource.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell) is our critic with respect to women's issues. One of the interesting aspects of this industry concerns the shore processing plants. It is very difficult for women who work seasonally and part time in those plants to earn a decent living. Would the Hon. Member outline some of the dilemmas that women face in this particular job ghetto area with parttime work, problems with unemployment insurance and, of course, the difficult question of secondary job area confinement?

Mr. Speaker, I hope Members of the House are aware of several cases, about two years ago, which went before the Unemployment Insurance Commission. These were concerns of women, equal partners in many cases, who go to sea in boats in very cold weather and carry an equal load in the job of fishing. They were treated as spouses or partners but were not treated equally with regard to paying into unemployment insurance. There was quite a protest. I believe that issue has now been resolved. Perhaps it is one on which we should

March 11, 1985
Fisheries Act
get an update to see how women feel about it at the present time.
I would suspect, just like family farming which involves women in several roles, that women in the fishing industry are the traditional homemakers and have responsibility for raising families. Women on farms work in the fields, particularly at harvest time, with their husbands and other farm workers. Most recently in the agricultural field, and I think the same could be said of the fisheries, they are having to take on extra jobs because there simply is not enough income. They are involved in full-time jobs quite often as well. This puts a triple workload on women. I hope the gentlemen in this House will realize that. This situation applies particularly to women in many resource areas.
I think my colleague is leading up to the question of part-time work as it affects women, because so often they are regarded as the secondary worker in a family. They are forced into part-time jobs, part-time jobs that do not have adequate benefits, that are not covered under the Labour Code. They should be covered under the Labour Code for pro-rated benefits. That is why we are pushing so hard for this provision for part-time workers, 73 per cent of whom are women. They are often the last hired and the first fired when there is a stress on jobs or when jobs are tight. I am sure this situation occurs in the fishery industry as well.
In my riding, as I mentioned, there are many women working in the fish plants. I have toured those plants. Those jobs are not very enviable in many ways. Quite often immigrant women are the ones who do these jobs. They do not speak very much English and often it is the only type of job they can get. It is important that they have decent pay, decently protected working conditions and job security.
In this industry the only way men and women and families can have job security is if the Government takes some positive steps to do more planning for renewal of stocks so we have more fish to fish and more fish to can and freeze. There will then be more opportunity for jobs in the processing of this particular resource.

Mr. Speaker, I have a comment. I have been listening with some interest to the speeches this morning. The speaker for the New Democratic Party suggested that there is no consultation going on. It could be construed as a big lie; if you say something often enough, it takes on a life of its own. Certainly in the fishing industry there has been conversation going on for years, any amount of it, but what has been lacking is action. Finally we have a Government and a Ministry that are prepared to take some action. The consultative process is in place. The Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Fraser) has advisory boards in place. Consultation will continue.
Concerning management of the fishery, let me speak about the herring roe industry where the fishing season is counted in hours, not in weeks or months. It is essential that Ministry officials have the opportunity to make decisions quickly.
There was conversation this morning about docks falling down in Newfoundland and in places elsewhere. There are a great many things that still need to be attended to in the operation of the fishery. The particular legislation before us is to give the Minister the opportunity to manage and to make decisions about allocation. That is a shortcoming in the present legislation. This is not meant to be a panacea for all the problems in the fishing industry. It is to address a particular aspect of it. It is long overdue and it is essential.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The period for questions and comments is now terminated. The Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) will resume debate.

Mr. Speaker, it was a pleasure to hear the comments made by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell), whose riding is next door to mine. I would like to start in French, because this Bill is of particular interest to the people of Quebec and to French-speaking Canadians on the West Coast who are affected by this legislation.
Mr. Speaker, in Clause 1 of the Bill, an addition is made to the definition of the term "fish". For instance, Clause 1.(1 )(a) provides, and I quote:
(a)	portions of fish,
(b)	... marine plants and portions thereof,
(c)	. .. shellfish, crustaceans and marine animals,
I see no problem with the definition and this addition.
In Clause 1.(2) the definition of "fishery" is also changed, and I quote:
"fishery" includes
(a)	the places in Canadian fisheries waters where, and the times when, fishing and related activities occur, including such packing, transporting and processing operations as are within the jurisdiction of Parliament, and
(b)	the persons engaged and the fishing vessels, fishing gear and other equipment used in the activities referred to in paragraph (a);"
Mr. Speaker, I have no problem with this definition, but there is a problem with "purposes" in Clause 2, and I quote:
2.1 The purposes of this Act are-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. Might I remind the Hon. Member that the debate on second reading is to be on the principle of the Bill and not on specific clauses as the Hon. Member seems to be doing.

I understand, Mr. Speaker. But the problem
with this Bill's principle may be found in this passage, and more specifically, in Clause 2.1(b), and I quote:
(b) to provide for the proper management, allocation and control of the seacoast fisheries of Canada;
I have a problem with the word "allocation". The Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Fraser) can only provide management for conservation, not for allocation.
*
March 11, 1985

There are many groups, including sports fishermen, commercial fishermen, Indians, etc. There may be as many as four or five different groups of fishermen, and that is the problem with this Bill. The Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Fraser) said recently that the Bill is the result of two court cases on which I would like to comment for a moment.
As I said, the problem is with the addition of allocation. It gives power to the Minister to allocate. It is to this that groups especialy on the Pacific coast object. There are a number of groups. For example, there are sports fishermen, commercial fishermen and the Indian fisheries. Within the different groups, say commercial fishermen, there are seiners, gillnetters and others. As long as the Minister had power to manage the fisheries for conservation purposes, it was accepted by the groups. However, a year or so ago the Minister was involved in two court cases as a result of the problem of allocating. In fact, in those court cases the Minister said that he would step in and say that sports fishermen could fish instead of commercial fishermen, or seiners instead of gillnetters. That was like putting the cat among the pigeons. There were complaints and two court cases.
I should like to comment on the court cases. The documents of the Department of Fisheries and Oceans indicate that the current Act is deficient in that it does not clearly give powers to the Minister to manage the fishery for economic and social purposes.

That was in the other passage, Mr. Speaker, in Clause 2.1, under "purposes", and I quote:
(c)	to ensure a continuing supply of fish and to maintain and develop the
economic and social benefits from the use of fish to fishermen-
The words "economic and social benefits"-

Economic and social concerns are new to the Act. We are adding to the main principle of the Act. My colleagues are saying that this is not mere housekeeping legislation. Once the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Fraser) is given the power to allocate stocks for economic and social reasons, we open up a can of worms, or perhaps a can of sardines in this particular case. It goes beyond the powers the Minister had before and it has ramifications. All user groups or fisher groups on the west coast raised some concerns.
The last Hon. Member who spoke indicated that there had been lots of consultation and that we should get on with action. I am a man of action. I like that approach. I respect the Minister of Fisheries who represents the next riding to mine. I have respected and know him for many years. He is a man of action. But we must remember that this is a bureaucracy with
6,000	people in it. As one of the fishermen said, if we could produce as much fish as we produce bureaucrats in the Department of Fisheries, we would be the leading nation in the world in fisheries. We have to be careful about the power we are giving the bureaucracy. The thrust of NDP speeches is that we want the Minister to give us a commitment to add to the
Fisheries Act
Bill or provide some other way for it to be done. Perhaps it could be discussed in committee. We want a consultative process to be written in so that the Minister cannot unilaterally or arbitrarily make allocations, especially when it is for social and economic purposes.
I am sure Hon. Members opposite admit that a lot can be done under those two words. We are saying that an industry consultative process should be set up. It would appeal to the Conservatie Party. As the Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell) said when she talked about what the United Fishermen and Allied Workers had told the NDP task force on jobs, Mr. Jack Nichol suggested that there should be set up a development board, which in fact would be the industry regulating the industry. I know that is difficult because in the past there have been disputes and different interests. However, they have one common interest: they are all in the fishing industry and they all want their fair share of it. It is a rich industry in Canada, especially on the west coast.
I should like to say something about the law in this respect. There were two rulings by Mr. Justice Collier of the Federal Court of Canada which indicated that the Department did not have the authority to allocate fish to various user groups, rendering management of the fishery in jeopardy on a national basis. In other words, Mr. Justice Collier's decisions show that the Department does not have the power to allocate fish to various user groups. If it is not possible to allocate to user groups, the Department's activities would be restricted to strictly opening and closing very global fisheries to all users. All it could do is open up the fishery or close it to all different users. It could not discriminate among users.
According to the Department of Fisheries and Oceans, this would result in the threat of overharvesting due to combined fishing power of users, and in hardship for many who would be denied access to the resources on the basis of specific allocation. The Department is saying that it cannot live with this situation because it opens it up too much and we could have overharvesting and so on. This has become more and more the argument of the Department.
I listened to the maiden speech of the new Member from Nanaimo. He said that we had to think about the fish-forget about the different users and preserve the fish. That is the basis of the new salmon treaty with the United States. When the Deputy Minister of the Department of Fisheries appeared before the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry, we asked him who won in the salmon treaty, and he said "the fish won". Everyone applauded because everyone likes the fish and it is nice that fish can win. The only problem is that we cannot take instructions from fish. We cannot consult the fish. Therefore, the Department of Fisheries and Oceans can say "this is what the fish want", meaning what it wants. I am not trying to be supercilious; it is always safe to say that we represent the fish, because the fish cannot talk back. We have to be careful with that line of argument, just as we have to be

March 11, 1985
Fisheries Act
careful with the line of argument that we should stop consulting and get on with some action. Let us protect the fish, let us have some action and so on, but let us do it in the proper way.
Mr. Justice Collier's decisions are worth looking at. The first case involved the Fishing Vessel Owners' Association of B.C., the Pacific Coast Salmon Seiners Association, the Prince Rupert Fishing Vessel Owners' Association, and the Department of Fisheries and Oceans. Mr. Justice Collier granted an injunction preventing the Department of Fisheries and Oceans from setting separate salmon quotas for seiners and gillnetters, prohibiting the Government from allocating the resource between the gear types. This is a case where the Department wanted to allocate for the seiners and gillnetters, not so much for conservation.
In case Hon. Members do not know this, I understand that the seiners put down a big net and scoop up the fish from the bottom. The gillnetters have a net that spreads out. The net of the seiners is like one steaming vegetables; you close the steamer in order to steam the vegetables. That is how the seiners work. The gillnetters have a net that spreads out; the salmon swim into it and catch their gills on it. That simple lesson is the difference between seiners and gillnetters. Mr. Justice Collier gave this interpretation. He said:
Strict interpretation of the Fisheries Act says all groups would have equal access to stocks over an equal area. The Act gives NFO the power to enforce regulations for the preservation and the conservation of the resource,-
As I said-

-to provide for the conservation and protection of fish. [English]
The Act does not give preference to one user group over another, for example, the seiners over the gillnetters. This is the principle or the crux of the Bill we are now debating. According to Mr. Justice Collier, the Fisheries Act and the Constitution Act-I gather that is the Constitution Act of 1982 and the British North America Act of 1876-Sections 91 and 92, set out the powers of the provincial Governments and the federal Government. Looking at these laws, Mr. Justice Collier said that the Government did not have the power to distinguish between one user group; that is, between the seiners and the gillnetters. Therefore, the Department could not act to exclude one from the fishery at a particular time, even by arguing that they really wanted to conserve the fish. What they were doing was deciding between two different groups.
That is why we have this amendment to give power to control on the basis of social and economic reasons, to develop the economic and social benefits flowing from the harvesting of fish.

To develop the economic and social benefits from the use of fish to fishermen and others-

The second case involved the Gulf Trollers Association of British Columbia against the Department of Fisheries and Oceans. In August, 1984 Mr. Justice Collier, the same judge, upheld the association's application to quash seven Government orders dated April 16 which permitted commercial fishing between July 1 and August 31, at the same time allowing sport fishing to operate year round. In effect, the Department was allocating the resource by giving preference to one group over another. Here the sport fishers were getting a preference over the commercial fishery. The Gulf Trollers Association, which is one of the commercial fishing groups in British Columbia, went to court and challenged the Department of Fisheries and Oceans.
In that case the judge did not accept the Department's argument that it has a federal power to manage and control the fisheries for the benefit of Canadians as distinct from the argument of preserving the stocks. Perhaps my friend who intervened last might be interested in the arguments by Crown counsel. Mr. Gunnar Eggertson, a distinguished counsel against whom the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and 1 have appeared in the Supreme Court in British Columbia at one time or another, was quoted by the Vancouver Sun. It quoted the court reported Mr. Eggertson's argument in court. He said:
Parliament has a duty to the people of Canada to manage the fishery and for the benefit of society and not for the benefit of the people who are in it.
The argument was that we represent the fish, not the people.
It was a decision made for a proper motive. The benefit of the fish and the people of Canada ... insisting that the Fisheries Department's power to manage included the power not to allow any fishing at all-
How to get user groups angry: just say: "Well, Your Lordship, as a matter of fact the Department could outlaw the fishery completely". I again quote Mr. Eggertson:
It is within the powers of the Government of Canada to restrict the troll fleet, even if there is no conservation consideration. There's no right for trollers to any season at all.
He said that we do not even have to bother about conservation, we can even tell them that they cannot fish at all. I do not know the right fishing analogy, but the farm analogy would be the red flag to the bull. No wonder they were angry at the Department. For court purposes, the Department took a pretty strong view, saying: "Forget it, we have complete power". Mr. Justice Collier said they do not have that kind of power at all. He said and I quote:
The April 16 variations of the total closure were, on the evidence presented by the Crown, conceived on two bases; a need for conservation and the intention to favour the sports fishers. The conservation motive was at the ultimate expense of the commercial gulf trollers. The preference. Collier stated, was based on socio-economic consideration which he considered to be beyond DFO's permissible constitutional powers.
How much time do I have left?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Hon. Member does not have any time left.

I will just wind up. I have outlined the two law cases. I have not been able to get into the constitutional
March 11, 1985

matter; the judge challenged the constitutionality. I am agreeable that these changes be made, frankly, with the consultation process.
Let us try and institute an industry consultation process so that the Department cannot do anything on the ground of socio-economic reasons. I do not think the Minister should take a reference on the constitutionality of the Fisheries Act. That would open up more problems. It is only a decision on an injunction, and I do not think he has to do that. I am replying to the debate I had with the Minister the other day. I hope he will read it in Hansard. In conclusion, our position is- [Translation]
-simply to hold consultations with all groups involved in fisheries here on the West Coast and on Canada's East Coast.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Questions or comments?

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Hon. Member a question. There is a problem which the Hon. Member recognizes as far as stock availability is concerned in practically every species off the British Columbia coast. He said that he is in agreement with the federal Government making decisions on socio-economic grounds and not just on the grounds of conservation and protection. We are into a new area here.
For purposes of argument, suppose there were five groups of salmon left over which could be caught off the British Columbia coast. Would the hon. gentleman allocate one to the trollers, one to the gillnetters, one to the seiners, one to the sports fishermen and one to the native population? That is what we are getting down to here. We are getting down to the allocation of a resource among user groups because there is not enough of that resource.
I do not know whether or not the question I put to the Hon. Member is unfair. He is not a Government Member. I just wonder about his opinion. Should each user group get an equal share of the resource or, when we get to the point where there is practically nothing left, which one do we erase? Do we erase the sports fishermen, the trollers, the seiners, the gillnetters? I would like the hon. gentleman to comment on that.

Mr. Speaker, hopefully we do not erase anyone and we do enhance the stock. This must be done through a consultation process with some fairness and equity in its management. I would ask the Hon. Member to be careful about how he quotes me. I said that the use of the phrase "social and economic terms" regarding allocation is very wide and that I have some real concerns about that which 1 would like to raise in committee.
Second, I said that if the resource must be allocated on the basis of the social and economic terms, then it must be done with safeguards, and the safeguard I suggested was to have the user groups decide co-operatively what should be done rather than have a distant Fisheries Department decide what should
Fisheries Act
be done. I also said that I recognize that that is not easy. The different groups have different interests and they have a history of arguing among themselves because they have different interests. I think I cited the suggestion of Jack Nichol which is that a Pacific fisheries development board be utilized in which all these groups could take part and have some say in the allocations.
I am optimistic. Everyone on the west coast recognizes that we have a resource that is dwindling. We also recognize that we need a fishing industry. Just as it is for those in the great province of Newfoundland, fishing is a part of the culture of those of us from British Columbia. Where would the province be without its salmon? I represent the only riding on the coast of British Columbia that does not border on the ocean and even I feel fishing and fishermen are very much a part of our culture on the coast.
While the fishermen may have conflicts, they are not stupid. They understand that they must work together and they will work together. Our Party has been suggesting that the resource be allocated over all by the Department but with built-in consultation with the user groups. I think that makes a lot of sense.

Mr. Speaker, I do not want to be unfair to the hon. gentleman. After all, he is not a Government Member. However, perhaps his Party does have a view on this question. I would like to repeat the question and narrow it down.
Suppose there was not enough of the resource for all of the user groups.
As a result of Liberal mismanagement?

The Hon. Member says that is the result of Liberal mismanagement. At this point in time, it does not matter who mismanaged the fishery; we have a problem on our hands. I would like to have an indication of the New Democratic Party's position on this important question.
Narrowing the question down further, if there is not enough of the resource left to maintain the user groups, would the Hon. Member and his Party advocate discontinuing the sports fishery? Does he regard the commercial fishery to be of more importance than the sports fishery in salmon, for example? I really would like to receive an answer to the question but I know that the hon. gentleman does not have to answer the question. Perhaps he does have some views on the issue of the sports fishermen versus the commercial fishermen when very little of that resource is left. Would he advocate a discontinuance of the commercial fishery in favour of the sports fishery?

Mr. Speaker, I do not understand why Liberal Members are so negative about this matter. Perhaps it is because of their years of mismanagement of the fishery. As I told the Hon. Member, I am not negative. He asked me what I would do if I were, God forbid, Minister of Fisheries of the country. I would concentrate on things like salmon enhancement on a huge scale. I would look at some of the things that are being done in Europe in the fish farming sector. I would

March 11, 1985
Fisheries Act
look to developing our industry the way it has been develop in Denmark, a country which I visited this summer and in which I saw what an efficient fishing industry can do.
It is purely hypothetical to talk about allocating five fish. There will not be five fish. Hopefully, there will be a great many fish. I admit that the different fishery groups are competing and that they have different interests, but they share one over-all interest and that is that they all benefit from the fishery. As I said before, fishermen are not stupid. They understand that.
I see the system working with more than simply the influence of the Minister's advisory committee which he calls on whim to consult when he wishes to consult. I would like to see something written into the legislation which would indicate that a Pacific fisheries development board would be involved. That board would be composed of the people who are most affected, not of some bureaucrats who are 3,000 miles away in Ottawa. I trust the people who are involved in the fishery industry in British Columbia to ultimately come up with suggestions for enhancement, allocation and so on. Naturally I feel that there must be a Fisheries Department in Ottawa to take part in all the different interests.
It is not a question of allocating five fish to five different groups. It is a question of managing an entire industry and having the people who are involved in the industry participate. I invite my friend, who I know has an open mind, to come toward this new social democracy which believes in decentralization, participation and co-operation and is very positive and new and is looking to the future. I invite him to come to the era of the 1990s and to throw out all that old baggage. Come on over here. We will have a new beginning and we will develop the fishery industries on the west coast and the east coast together.

Mr. Speaker, one of the interesting aspects of this Bill is the question of its constitutionality. We could allow this Bill to pass through the House of Commons and it could be put in place, but what would happen if, in the middle of the salmon season this coming summer, a dissatisfied fisherman on the west coast suddenly took the matter to court, said this is against the constitution and the Federal Court granted an injunction against the fishing plan and threw this amendment out of court? A judge from the Federal Court has indicated that this could happen and the Government has indicated that this could happen.
Would there be merit in putting this Bill through the House with the Minister's guidelines and mechanisms for consultation and referring it to the Supreme Court so it may make a judgment as to whether or not this Bill will stand up constitutionally? I wonder if my hon. colleague might give us an indication of whether it might be wise to do so at this point or wait until the season collapses this summer.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Could I ask for a short answer from the Hon. Member for Vancouver Kingsway (Mr. Waddell)?

Mr. Speaker, I draw the Hon. Member's attention to the statement made by the Minister on March 6, 1985, as reported on page 2789 of Hansard. To be very fair to the Minister, this is a problem with which the Minister must struggle. The Minister got out of these two court cases by having us amend this law but he cannot get out of the constitutionality question.
I do not think I would like to give a quick answer to this question. I think we should hear from the Minister in committee. As my friend pointed out, there will be problems if someone challenges this in the middle of the season. I think that must be considered in committee.
I have already given my own opinion as a constitutional lawyer. I would not like to see the Minister give this matter a quick reference to the court. I would prefer to have him wait, but I could be persuaded otherwise.
